# Bone tissue

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Endocrinology > Basics of endocrinology and metabolism > Bone tissue*

[Original Article Link](/library/Ho0KWS)

---

## Summary

The <u>musculoskeletal system</u> is comprised of bones and <u>connective tissue</u> structures, such as <u>cartilage</u>, <u>ligaments</u>, and <u>tendons</u>. These structures are brought into motion by <u>skeletal muscles</u>. To withstand resultant forces, bone tissue resists pressure and tension and is minimally elastic. Bone tissue mainly consists of <u>bone cells</u> (<u>osteoblasts</u>, <u>osteocytes</u>, and <u>osteoclasts</u>) and a mineralized <u>extracellular matrix</u> that is primarily made up of <u>collagen fibrils</u> and <u>hydroxyapatite</u> crystals. <u>Ossification</u>, or bone formation, begins with a framework that consists of either <u>mesenchymal</u> <u>connective tissue</u> (<u>intramembranous ossification</u>) or <u>cartilage</u> (<u>endochondral ossification</u>). <u>Woven bone</u> is formed, which is replaced by the more solid and layered <u>lamellar bone</u>. The outer cortical layers can be macroscopically differentiated from the branched center of the trabeculae.

---

## Overview

### Function of bone




* Supportive function

* Protective function

* Storage (<u>calcium</u> and <u>phosphorus</u> reservoir)

* <u>Hematopoiesis</u>





### Types of bone




* Long bones: include the <u>femur</u>, <u>humerus</u>, <u>ulna</u>, radius, <u>fibula</u>, <u>tibia</u>, <u>metacarpals</u>, and <u>phalanges</u>  

* Epiphysis

* Consists of <u>compact bone</u> that surrounds <u>trabecular bone</u>

* <u>Proximal</u> or <u>distal</u> end of a <u>long bone</u> with its trabeculae aligned along the lines of <u>stress</u>

* Linear growth of <u>long bones</u> in children and adults occurs in the <u>epiphysis</u> (<u>epiphyseal plate</u>).

* Contains the articular surface of bones

* Metaphysis: area between the <u>epiphysis</u> and the <u>diaphysis</u>

* Diaphysis

* Shaft of a <u>long bone</u> (central region)

* Consists of <u>compact bone</u> and the <u>medullary cavity</u> where the <u>bone marrow</u> is stored

* Apophysis: large bony projections where <u>ligaments</u> and <u>tendons</u> attach

* Short bones: include tarsal and <u>carpal bones</u>

* Flat bones  

* Include the <u>scapulae</u>, <u>sternum</u>, <u>ribs</u>, and most bones of the <u>skull</u>

* Composed of two layers of <u>compact bone</u> that surrounds <u>trabecular bone</u> and <u>bone marrow</u>

* Sesamoid bones

* Bones that develop within <u>tendons</u> (e.g., the patella)

* Function to reduce friction of the <u>tendon</u> and to reduce excessive wear

* Irregular bones  

* Include the <u>sacrum</u>, <u>coccyx</u>, <u>vertebrae</u>, <u>mandible</u>, palatine, hyoid, and <u>temporal bones</u>

* Have several functions including:

* Attachment for the <u>tendon</u> of muscles

* Protection (e.g., <u>vertebrae</u> protect the spinal cord)

## Bone composition

### Overview




The exact composition or organization of individual bone components differs in the various bones types and maturation stages. All human bones are composed of the same basic elements:




* <u>Bone cells</u>: build and remodel bones

* <u>Bone matrix</u>: composed of organic and inorganic components

* <u>Bone membranes</u>: cover the inner and outer surface of the bone

* <u>Bone marrow</u>: either actively involved in <u>hematopoiesis</u> (<u>red bone marrow</u>) or primarily replaced by adipose cells (<u>yellow bone marrow</u>)





### Bone cells




| Characteristics of <u>bone cells</u> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | Definition | <br>Function [[3]](/library/1PY2d6) | Location |
| Osteoprogenitor cells | <br>* Barely differentiated precursor <u>bone cells</u> that originate from the <u>mesenchyme</u><br><br> | <br>* Differentiate into and replace <u>osteoblasts</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Periosteum</u> and <u>endosteum</u><br><br> |
| <br>Osteoblasts [[4]](/library/xhYETK) | <br>* Bone-building cells that differentiate from <u>osteoprogenitor cells</u><br><br>* Stimulated by <u>transforming growth factor-beta</u> (<u>TGF-β</u>), and bone morphogenic <u>proteins</u><br><br>* Have <u>receptors</u> for <u>PTH</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Produce osteoid (organic <u>bone matrix</u>, mainly composed of <u>collagen</u>), which is stored in layers on the mineralized matrix<br><br>* Require alkaline environment (↑ <u>pH</u>) for bone alkaline phosphatase (<u>ALP</u>), an enzyme that cleaves inorganic <u>phosphate</u> from various substrates to make it available for mineralization<br><br>* Control <u>osteoid</u> mineralization (<u>hydroxyapatite</u> formation)<br><br>* Regulate <u>bone remodeling</u><br><br><br> | <br>* On free bony surfaces of the <u>periosteum</u> and <u>endosteum</u><br><br> |
| Osteocytes | <br>* Star-shaped <u>osteoblasts</u> with long, <u>cytoplasmic</u> processes located deep within the lacunae, on which a new <u>osteoid</u> layer has been deposited<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Bone remodeling</u><br><br>* See “<u>Bone remodeling</u>” and “<u>Regulation of bone remodeling</u>” below for more details.<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Distributed throughout the mineralized <u>bone matrix</u> (in bone cavities, lacunae)<br><br>* Connected to surrounding <u>osteoblasts</u> and <u>osteocytes</u> through <u>gap junctions</u> (<u>macula communicans</u>) in the bone canaliculi<br><br><br> |
| Osteoclasts | <br><br>* Bone-dissolving multinucleated <u>phagocytes</u> that degrade mineralized bone<br><br>* Derive from the fusion of <u>monocyte</u> and <u>macrophage</u> precursor cells<br><br>* Have <u>calcitonin</u> <u>receptors</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Bone remodeling</u> and bone resorption (osteolysis)<br><br>* See “<u>Bone remodeling</u>” and “<u>Regulation of bone remodeling</u>” below for more details.<br><br><br> | <br>* Distributed in the bone in <u>Howship lacunae</u> and bone multicellular units<br><br> |





### Bone matrix




Composed of organic and inorganic material:




* Organic

* <u>Type 1 collagen</u>

* Ground substances: <u>chondroitin sulfate</u> and <u>keratan sulfate</u>

* Glycoproteins (e.g., osteocalcin, osteopontin) and <u>proteoglycans</u>: bind to <u>hydroxyapatite</u> and to <u>integrin</u> molecules on <u>osteoclasts</u> and <u>osteoblasts</u>

* Inorganic

* Hydroxyapatite: <u>hydroxylated</u> <u>calcium</u> <u>phosphate</u> salts that adhere to <u>collagen fibrils</u> in a crystallized form and increase resistance to pressure

* Various ions (e.g., <u>calcium</u>, <u>phosphate</u>, <u>magnesium</u>, <u>bicarbonate</u>, <u>citrate</u>, <u>potassium</u>, and <u>fluoride</u>)





### Bone membranes




* Periosteum: a membrane of <u>connective tissue</u> that covers the outer surface of the bone in two distinct layers 

* Cambium layer: inner vascular and innervated layer (very sensitive to <u>pain</u>) that is lined with <u>bone cells</u>

* Fibrous layer: outer layer consisting of <u>connective tissue</u> from which Sharpey fibers extend into the bone

* Endosteum

* A membrane that lines the inner surface of the bone (e.g., <u>trabecular bone</u> or <u>Haversian canal</u>)

* Composition: thin (nonmineralized) layer of <u>collagen</u> lined with <u>bone cells</u>





> [!NOTE]
> The <u>periosteum</u> and the <u>endosteum</u> consist of the same type of <u>bone cells</u>.




### <u>Bone marrow</u>




* <u>Red bone marrow</u> (<u>hematopoietic</u>): primarily in the short and <u>flat bones</u> and partly in the <u>epiphyses</u> of the <u>long bones</u> in adults

* <u>Yellow bone marrow</u> (fat storage): primarily fills the medullary cavities of the <u>long bones</u> in adults

* For more details on <u>bone marrow</u>, see “<u>Basics of hematology</u>”.

---

## Development and maturation

### Development of bone



* Bone is derived from <u>mesoderm</u>.

* <u>Axial skeleton</u> arises from <u>paraxial mesoderm</u>.

* <u>Appendicular skeleton</u> arises from the <u>lateral plate mesoderm</u>.




#### Ossification




| Overview of the <u>ossification</u> process |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | <br>Endochondral ossification<br> | Intramembranous ossification |
| Definition | <br>* Bone is indirectly formed from <u>mesenchymal</u> cells via the <u>cartilaginous model</u> in the <u>diaphysis</u> of bones.<br><br> | <br>* Bone is formed directly from <u>mesenchymal</u> <u>connective tissue</u> (no <u>cartilaginous model</u>).<br><br> |
| Process | <br>* <u>Mesenchymal</u> cells differentiate to <u>chondroblasts</u> → formation of a cartilaginous model<br><br>* Bone collar formation: Bone forms around the <u>cartilaginous model</u>.<br>1. * <u>Mesenchymal</u> cells differentiate into <u>chondroblasts</u> → formation of a <u>cartilaginous model</u> with <u>perichondrium</u><br>2. * <u>Osteoblasts</u> develop in the <u>perichondrium</u> and form a bone collar around the <u>cartilaginous</u> <u>diaphysis</u> (similar to <u>membranous ossification</u>).<br>3. * The <u>perichondrium</u> transforms into <u>periosteum</u>.<br><br>* Bone formation within the <u>cartilaginous model</u><br>1. * <u>Cartilage</u> cells in the bone collar become <u>hypertrophic</u> and initiate mineralization of the <u>cartilaginous</u> matrix.<br>2. * Infiltration of <u>blood vessels</u> and <u>osteoprogenitor cells</u> through canals<br>3. * <u>Osteoclasts</u> from the <u>periosteum</u> break down the <u>cartilaginous</u> matrix.<br>4. * Chondroclasts start to degrade <u>cartilage</u> in the center of the bone → medullary cavity formation<br>5. * Increased <u>apoptosis</u> of <u>hypertrophic</u> <u>chondrocytes</u><br>6. * <u>Osteoblasts</u> and <u>osteoclasts</u> replace <u>cartilaginous</u> matrix with bone tissue (woven bone → <u>lamellar bone</u>).<br>7. * The process proceeds in the direction of both <u>epiphyses</u> → two progressive <u>ossification</u> zones<br><br> | <br>1. * <u>Mesenchymal</u> cells differentiate into <u>osteoblasts</u> at the <u>ossification</u> center.<br>2. * <u>Osteoblasts</u> deposit osteoids → <u>osteocytes</u> form after <u>osteoid</u> mineralization → formation of a bone segment<br>3. * The <u>osteoblasts</u> on the outer surface of the bone segment deposit <u>osteoid</u> layers → <u>appositional growth</u><br>4. * Several bone segments fuse to primary <u>trabecular bone</u>.<br>5. * <u>Blood vessels</u> and undifferentiated <u>mesenchymal</u> cells invade the trabecular bone → formation of <u>bone marrow</u><br>6. * Simultaneous construction and remodeling of bone (woven bone → <u>lamellar bone</u>)<br>7. * <u>Mesenchymal</u> layers that do not become ossified → formation of <u>endosteum</u> and <u>periosteum</u><br><br> |
| Examples | <br>* Bones of the limbs, <u>axial skeleton</u> (<u>vertebrae</u> and <u>ribs</u>), <u>base of the skull</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Facial bones</u> (e.g., <u>mandible</u>), parts of the <u>calvarium</u>, <u>clavicle</u><br><br> |





> [!NOTE]
> The <u>skull</u> undergoes both processes: some bones (e.g., frontal, <u>parietal bones</u>) are derived from the <u>neural crest</u> and undergo <u>membranous ossification</u>, whereas other bones (e.g., <u>sphenoid</u>, occipital bones) are derived from the <u>paraxial mesoderm</u> and undergo <u>endochondral ossification</u>.

### <u>Stages of bone maturity</u>




Bones are arranged into <u>woven bone</u> (primary bone) during <u>embryonic development</u> or <u>bone healing</u>. The structure of <u>woven bone</u> is disorganized and transformed into organized tissue of <u>lamellar bone</u> (secondary bone) through continuous remodeling.




| Stages of bone maturity |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | Woven bone | <br>Lamellar bone<br> |
| Definition | <br>* Immature bone that is formed during <u>fetal development</u> and <u>bone healing</u><br><br> | <br>* Mature bone formed by remodeling of <u>woven bone</u><br><br> |
| <u>Histology</u> | <br><br>* Disorganized <u>collagen fibers</u><br><br>* Less mineralized bone substance with a high water content<br><br>* Rich in cells<br><br><br> | <br>* The <u>extracellular matrix</u> is organized into two types of tissues:<br><br>* <u>Trabecular bone</u> (see “<u>Trabecular bone</u>” below)<br><br>* <u>Cortical bone</u> (see “<u>Cortical bone</u>” below)<br><br> |
| Characteristics | <br><br>* Mechanically weaker and more flexible than <u>lamellar bone</u><br><br>* Formed during <u>embryonic development</u>, after <u>fractures</u> (<u>secondary bone healing</u>), and in Paget disease<br><br><br> | <br>* Mechanically strong<br><br> |
| Remodeling | <br>* Usually successively remodeled to more stable lamellar bones<br><br> | <br>* Load-dependent, continuous remodeling of bone according to acting forces<br><br> |





> [!NOTE]
> The direction of <u>collagen fibers</u> of the bone <u>extracellular matrix</u> is an important distinguishing characteristic between immature <u>woven bone</u> and mature <u>lamellar bone</u>.




![Lamellar bone](media/onmgfwhsdwcz8az6zaikqtvl.jpg)

Lamellar bone

![Lamellar bone](media/myf7si2leex4mzmuzje7vumy.jpg)

Lamellar bone




#### Trabecular bone (spongy or <u>cancellous bone</u>)




* Definition: thin lattice-shaped (trabeculae) units inside the <u>lamellar bone</u>

* Characteristics

* Trabeculae are aligned along large compressive and tensile forces (trajectory direction).

* The <u>bone marrow</u> is located in the intermediate space of the <u>trabecular bone</u>.





![Spongy bone with red marrow](media/wffexoegeiwtr0jbqv7vaz4y.jpg)

Spongy bone with red marrow




#### Cortical bone (<u>compact bone</u>)




* Definition: homogeneous and dense cortical layer of <u>lamellar bone</u>

* Main components

* Osteon

* Definition: concentric bony lamellae with a central <u>Haversian canal</u>

* Direction: several concentric lamellae whose <u>collagen fibers</u> change direction from one lamella to the other

* Boundary: cement lines

* Interstitial lamellae

* Remnants of partially destroyed <u>osteons</u>

* Separate <u>osteons</u> from one another

* Circumferential lamellae: provide an outer and inner boundary for the <u>cortical bone</u> through at least one lamellar layer





#### Lamellar bones vascularization and canals



* Bone canals and associated vessels

* Haversian canal: a canal in the center of the <u>osteon</u> that contains Haversian vessels, which supply the bone with blood

* Volkmann canal (perforating channels): canals radiating from the <u>periosteum</u> that are at a right angle to <u>Haversian vessels</u> and are supplied by Volkmann vessels




> [!NOTE]
> The course of <u>lamellar bone</u> vessels is strictly defined by the Haversian and Volkmann canal structures. In contrast, <u>woven bone</u> vessels are disorganized.




![Osteons with Haversian canals](media/hg2o7l58sru7fhxoxg28l92c.jpg)

Osteons with Haversian canals




### Development of <u>long bones</u>




* Primary ossification center: <u>diaphysis</u>
1. * <u>Bone collar formation</u>
2. * <u>Endochondral ossification</u>

* Secondary ossification center: <u>epiphysis</u> 

* Time period: shortly before or after <u>birth</u>

* Process: <u>endochondral ossification</u>, similar to diaphyseal

* Nonossifying segments

* <u>Joint</u> surfaces

* <u>Epiphyseal plate</u>

* Longitudinal growth of the <u>long bones</u>
1. * <u>Chondrocyte</u> proliferate at the <u>epiphyseal plates</u> → longitudinal growth with the <u>epiphysis</u> pushed away from the <u>diaphysis</u>
2. * <u>Cartilage</u> tissue is degraded and remodeled in bone tissue from the <u>medullary cavity</u>.
3. * The <u>proliferation zone</u> progresses with the same <u>velocity</u> as the <u>ossification zone</u>.
4. * <u>Chondrocytes</u> cease proliferating and bone replaces <u>cartilage</u> (<u>ossification zone</u>) in a process known as epiphyseal fusion.





![Ossification of long bones](media/iyak8ag3sui1bofta15mtcrw.jpg)

Ossification of long bones




#### Epiphyseal plate




The part of the bone where longitudinal growth takes place. Layers include (from <u>epiphysis</u> to <u>diaphysis</u>):



1. * Zone of resting cartilage: deposits undifferentiated precursor <u>chondrocytes</u> that provide the <u>proliferation zone</u> with new <u>chondrocytes</u>
2. * Proliferation zone: <u>mitosis</u> of <u>chondrocytes</u>

* <u>Proliferation</u> process

* Isogenic <u>chondrocytes</u> are vertically stacked on top of one another (each <u>chondrocyte</u> lies in a separate lacuna).

* In the column, the <u>chondrocytes</u> mature in the direction of growth.

* <u>Chondrocytes</u> enlarge and produce an <u>extracellular matrix</u>.

* <u>Chondrocyte</u> separation

* Vertical (from an isogenic neighbor): transverse septum

* Horizontal (from nonisogenic neighbors): longitudinal septum
3. * Zone of hypertrophy: enlarges <u>cartilage</u> through <u>chondrocyte</u> <u>hypertrophy</u>, which leads to <u>collagen</u> (type X) production by <u>hypertrophic</u> <u>chondrocytes</u> and mineralization of the longitudinal septa
4. * Zone of calcification

* Functions

* Opening of the <u>cartilaginous</u> lacunae by removal of the transverse septa

* <u>Apoptosis</u> of <u>hypertrophic</u> <u>chondrocytes</u>

* Process

* Secretion of <u>VEGF</u> and <u>matrix metalloproteinases</u> by <u>chondrocytes</u>

* <u>Blood vessels</u> and <u>macrophages</u> migrate → transverse septa erode

* Effects

* Mineralized columns remain (ossified longitudinal septa).

* Approx. ⅓ of the longitudinal septa is retained, and the remaining septa is degraded by chondroclasts.
5. * Zone of ossification: <u>colonization</u> of the mineralized longitudinal septae by <u>osteoblasts</u> → <u>osteoid</u> formation → mineralization




![Epiphyseal plate](media/ykjx73chw6rvl44yaetwawyb.jpg)

Epiphyseal plate

![Hyaline cartilage](media/bakmna09i2pyao3psyjaalfy.jpg)

Hyaline cartilage

## Bone remodeling and healing

The human skeleton is in a continuous dynamic state of remodeling. Not only does this apply to the replacement of immature <u>woven bone</u> by <u>lamellar bone</u>, but also for adaptation of adult bones to their individual load.





### Bone remodeling [[6]](/library/yhYdgK)




* Cells involved

* <u>Osteoclasts</u>: degrade bone tissue by secreting <u>collagenase</u> and H<sup>+</sup>

* <u>Osteoblasts</u>

* Build bone tissue by secreting <u>type I collagen</u>

* Activity assessed by an increase in bone <u>ALP</u>, <u>osteocalcin</u>, and type I <u>procollagen</u> propeptides

* Duration: usually longer than the lifespan of the cells involved  (continual replacement of involved cells)





> [!NOTE]
> Blasts Build, Clasts Crumble.




![Bone remodeling](media/g0a9cwqnigf7g6ni6hymk7un.jpg)

Bone remodeling




#### <u>Bone remodeling</u> in <u>cortical bone</u>




* Degradation

* <u>Osteoclasts</u> organize in a basic multicellular unit (<u>BMU</u>) and excavate a tunnel in the <u>cortical bone</u>.

* <u>Connective tissue</u> vessels and unmyelinated nerves grow in the tunnel.

* Formation

* <u>Osteoclasts</u> are followed by <u>osteoblasts</u> → deposition of the first <u>osteoid</u> layer in the tunnel

* Additional <u>osteoblasts</u> follow and deposit <u>osteoid</u> onto the first <u>osteoid</u> layer → <u>osteoblasts</u> of the first layer are walled in → <u>osteoblasts</u> become <u>osteocytes</u>

* The deposition process is repeated until the tunnel is almost full → central <u>Haversian canal</u> remains open

* The innermost (i.e., last) generation of <u>osteoblasts</u> is no longer walled in → cells return to their resting state and form the <u>endosteum</u>

* Mineralization: occurs successively

* <u>Osteoblasts</u> secrete <u>collagen</u> and <u>vesicles</u> into the <u>extracellular matrix</u>.

* <u>Vesicles</u> contain enzymes (e.g., <u>alkaline phosphatase</u>), which increase local <u>phosphate</u> levels (e.g., by cleavage of <u>pyrophosphate</u>).

* <u>Calcium</u>-binding molecules in the <u>vesicles</u> most likely serve as a <u>focal point</u>.

* Initial formation of <u>hydroxyapatite</u> crystals around the <u>focal point</u> in the <u>vesicles</u>

* Independent growth of the crystals until penetration of the <u>vesicle</u> membrane

* Release of crystals in the <u>extracellular matrix</u>

* Growth of crystals in the <u>extracellular matrix</u> and accumulation of <u>collagen fibrils</u>





#### <u>Bone remodeling</u> in <u>trabecular bone</u>




* Degradation

* <u>Osteoclasts</u> organize in Howship lacunae (small depressions on the <u>trabecular bone</u> surface). They move to resorb <u>trabecular bone</u> and form a tight seal around the resorption area.

* <u>Osteoclasts</u> produce protons via the enzyme <u>carbonic anhydrase</u>.

* Secretion of <u>chloride ions</u> (passive) and protons (active, via ATPase) in <u>Howship lacunae</u>, with the formation of an acidic environment (∼ <u>pH</u> 4.5) → dissolution of inorganic bone elements

* Secretion of <u>lysosomal</u> enzymes (especially <u>cathepsin</u> K and <u>matrix metalloproteinases</u>) → degradation of organic bone elements

* <u>Endocytosis</u>/transcytosis of the bone elements

* Formation

* Filling of the gaps with groups of <u>osteoblasts</u> → walled in under each lamella (then termed <u>osteocytes</u>)

* The last group of <u>osteoblasts</u> remains as a part of the <u>endosteum</u> on the bone surface.





### Regulation of bone remodeling [[7]](/library/AhYRgK)




* RANK (<u>receptor activator of nuclear factor κB</u>): <u>receptor</u> on <u>osteoclasts</u> and <u>osteoclast</u> precursors, for interaction with <u>osteoblasts</u>

* RANKL (<u>receptor activator of nuclear factor κB ligand</u>)

* Membrane-bound protein of <u>osteoblasts</u> that stimulates <u>osteoclasts</u> by interacting with <u>RANK</u>

* Ensures fusion and differentiation into activated <u>osteoclasts</u> and prevents their <u>apoptosis</u>

* Osteoprotegerin (<u>OPG</u>)

* A <u>regulatory protein</u> secreted by <u>osteoblasts</u> that binds <u>RANKL</u>

* Inhibits <u>RANK</u>-<u>RANKL</u> interaction, leading to decreased <u>osteoclast</u> activity

* <u>M-CSF</u> (<u>macrophage colony-stimulating factor</u>)

* Secreted by <u>osteoblasts</u>

* Promotes the <u>proliferation</u> of <u>osteoclast</u> precursor cells

* Simultaneous binding and fusion of <u>M-CSF</u> and <u>RANKL</u> on the surface of precursor <u>osteoclasts</u> on the <u>synovium</u> → differentiation of precursor <u>osteoclasts</u> into <u>osteoclasts</u>

* Mechanical load 

* Load on the bone leads to increased <u>bone mass</u>.

* Absence of load (e.g., due to being confined in bed) results in decreased <u>bone mass</u>.

* Negative feedback by <u>osteoclasts</u>: growth factors are embedded in the <u>bone matrix</u> and are released during degradation by <u>osteoclasts</u> → <u>osteoblasts</u> stimulation

* <u>Hormones</u>

* <u>PTH</u> effects

* At low levels: increased bone formation and increased <u>apoptosis</u> of <u>osteoclasts</u> → decreased bone resorption (<u>anabolic</u> effects)

* At high levels (e.g., <u>primary hyperparathyroidism</u>): activation of <u>osteoclasts</u> → increased bone resorption (<u>catabolic</u> effects) → <u>osteoporosis</u> or <u>osteitis fibrosa cystica</u>

* <u>Estrogen</u> effects

* Inhibits <u>apoptosis</u> of <u>osteoblasts</u>, leading to increased bone formation

* Stimulates <u>apoptosis</u> of <u>osteoclasts</u>, leading to decreased bone resorption

* Stimulates closure of the <u>epiphyseal plate</u> in <u>puberty</u>

* <u>Estrogen deficiency</u> (e.g., <u>postmenopausal</u> or after bilateral <u>oophorectomy</u>) leads to increased bone resorption, which can result in <u>osteoporosis</u>.

* <u>Vitamin D</u>

* Stimulates <u>osteoblasts</u> and <u>osteoclast</u> differentiation

* Activation of <u>osteoblasts</u> → increased bone formation and mineralization

* Medication

* <u>Bisphosphonates</u> inhibit <u>osteoclasts</u> → used to treat <u>osteoporosis</u>

* <u>Glucocorticoids</u> increase <u>osteoclast</u> lifespan → increased bone resorption





> [!NOTE]
> <u>Estrogen</u> has a positive effect on bone balance because it inhibits <u>osteoclast</u> formation and activation and increases <u>OPG</u> formation.




![Effects of RANK, RANKL, and OPG in the regulation of bone remodeling](media/twehfqkf7majnx8daob8dw8x.jpg)

Effects of RANK, RANKL, and OPG in the regulation of bone remodeling




### Bone healing [[8]](/library/_hY5gK)




<u>Fractures</u> occur when bones are strained beyond their maximum load. <u>Fractures</u> can heal in two different ways.




* Primary bone healing

* Occurs when the broken ends of the bone are very close together (interval < 1 mm), e.g., when surgically fixed

* <u>Lamellar bone</u> can be directly formed in the <u>fracture</u> gap (gap healing).

* Secondary bone healing

* Occurs when the distance of the <u>fracture</u> ends is larger

* Initial bridging of the <u>fracture</u> gap is formed with <u>connective tissue</u> or <u>cartilage</u> (fibrocartilage callus).

* Conversion to <u>woven bone</u> (bony callus) by <u>endochondral ossification</u>

* Over the course of months, <u>woven bone</u> is slowly remodeled into resilient <u>lamellar bone</u>.

* <u>Pseudoarthrosis</u>: can occur if the healing process is permanently disturbed by motion of the <u>fracture</u> ends (e.g., through insufficient <u>immobilization</u>)





> [!NOTE]
> During childhood or <u>adolescence</u>, a <u>fracture</u> near a <u>joint</u> may damage the unclosed <u>epiphyseal plate</u>, which can result in growth disorders (e.g., asymmetry, inhibition, <u>acceleration</u>) during healing.
> 
> References:[[9]](/library/U30b3f)[[10]](/library/Lvaw05)

* <u>Osteoporosis</u>

* <u>Osteomalacia</u> and <u>rickets</u>

* Paget disease

* <u>Fractures</u>

## Radiographic signs of malignant bone tumors

* Margins of the lesion: The more poorly defined the margins of the lesion are, the more rapid is the <u>tumor</u> growth. [[11]](/library/fQ0kvf)

* Type I: geographic

* Type II: moth-eaten appearance

* Type III: permeative

* Periosteal reactions: reactive periosteal bone synthesis as a result of bone destruction by a malignant process  [[12]](/library/TQ06vf)





![Periosteal reactions in malignant bone tumors](media/p3kph42kzcbnqxsmhpjj3f8w.jpg)

Periosteal reactions in malignant bone tumors




### Types of <u>periosteal reactions</u>[[12]](/library/TQ06vf)




* Continuous <u>periosteal reactions</u>

* Solid periosteal reaction

* Increased formation of new bone, with or without cortical destruction

* Indicates slow <u>tumor</u> growth

* Lamellated periosteal reaction

* Multiple layers of new bone (<u>onion skin appearance</u>)

* Indicates rapid <u>tumor</u> growth

* Spiculated periosteal reaction

* <u>Spicules</u> (new bone formations) that grow along Sharpey fibers (<u>collagen fibers</u> that anchor the <u>periosteum</u> to the <u>compact bone</u>)

* Indicates more aggressive <u>tumor</u> growth compared to the solid and lamellated types

* <u>Hair-on-end appearance</u>: <u>spicules</u> that extend perpendicular to the bone surface

* Sunburst appearance: divergent <u>spicules</u> that resemble a sunburst

* Interrupted <u>periosteal reactions</u>

* Occur if continuous <u>periosteal reactions</u> are themselves disturbed by <u>tumor</u> growth

* Indicate the presence of a particularly aggressive malignant process

* Codman triangle: develops as a result of the destruction and elevation of singular or multiple periosteal lamellae
